questions_and_answers.question: Which case does a German pronoun take when it acts as the subject (the actor in a sentence)?
In German, the pronouns mich, uns, ihn etc. belong to which case?
Which pronoun form is used to designate the interested bystander or indirect object in German?
If a pronoun follows the preposition 'mit', which case must it take?
In the substitution principle, when substituting a pronoun in a sentence like 'Er kennt mich', which forms can replace 'mich'?
Which pronoun forms correspond to the first person singular in the nominative, accusative and dative cases?
How does German express the English progressive aspect (e.g., 'he's singing')?

answers.answer: It uses the simple verb form without an -ing equivalent
It uses a verb ending in -ing

questions_and_answers.question: What is the special characteristic of the verbs arbeiten and kosten in the er-form?

answers.answer: They require a connecting vowel -e- before the ending -t
They change their vowel in the stem
They take an -s ending like the English he-form

questions_and_answers.question: Which words are added to 'wo' to mean 'where from?' and 'where to?' respectively?

answers.answer: her for 'where from?' and hin for 'where to?'
hin for 'where from?' and her for 'where to?'

questions_and_answers.question: Where does the infinitive appear in a German verb phrase like 'Ich kann gehen'?

answers.answer: At the end of the sentence and unaffected by subject

articles.text:
Notes on Grammar (For Home Study)
A. Pronouns – Forms and functions.
I. Forms.
In the following English sentences the pronouns are underlined. Note their forms. Most English pronouns have two different forms: I-me, he-him, she-her, etc. Some, like you and it, have only one form however.

Note the forms of the German pronouns in the following sentences:
Verstehen Sie mich?
Ja, ich verstehe Sie gut.
Wie geht es Ihnen?
Er spricht englisch mit mir.
Some German pronouns have two different forms, like Sie and Ihnen above. Many German pronouns however have three different forms like ich, mich and mir.

The following table gives the forms of the most common German pronouns:
Nominative forms:
ich, wir, er, es, sie, sie, Sie, wer, was
Accusative forms:
mich, uns, ihn, es, sie, sie, Sie, wen, was
Dative forms:
mir (me), uns (us), ihm (him), ihm (it), ihr (her), ihnen (them), Ihnen (you), wem (whom?), was (what?)
The English forms at the top of the table correspond to the set of German forms above the line. Those at the bottom of the table correspond to the two sets of German forms below the line. The pronouns wer and was are used only in questions. The pronouns for familiar address, du and ihr, will be taken up later.

II. Functions.
The NOMINATIVE form: In German, as in English, the basic sentence structure is an ACTOR-ACTION pattern: somebody doing something. The ACTOR is called the SUBJECT of the sentence, and in German a pronoun designating the ACTOR always has the NOMINATIVE form.
Ich verstehe sehr gut.
Er wohnt ganz in meiner Nähe.
Wir wollen gerade essen gehen.
I understand very well. He lives quite near me. We’re just planning to go and eat.

The ACCUSATIVE form: In many sentences in both English and German there is another element, the GOAL or OBJECT of the action, the person or thing toward which the action is aimed. In German a pronoun designating the OBJECT of an action is usually in the ACCUSATIVE form.
Ich kenne ihn sehr gut.
Verstehen Sie mich?
Wir treffen sie dort.
I know him very well. Do you understand me? We’re meeting them (or her) there.

The DATIVE form: The third form of the German pronoun is used to designate the INTERESTED BYSTANDER, the person to whom or for whom or with regard to whom the action of the sentence is being performed. In some cases this is referred to as the INDIRECT OBJECT.
Können Sie mir seine Adresse geben?
Sie müssen ihm Ihren Pass zeigen.
Wie geht es Ihnen?
Gefällt es Ihnen in München?
Der Koffer gehört mir nicht.
Can you give me his address? You have to show him your passport. How are you? Do you like it in Munich? The suitcase doesn’t belong to me.

Another use of the DATIVE form is illustrated by the following sentences:
Sprechen Sie englisch mit ihr?
Ich fahre oft mit ihm nach Hause.
Do you speak English with her? I often ride home with him.
The DATIVE forms ihr and ihm are used here because they follow the word mit, and that’s all there is to it. Any pronoun that follows mit has the DATIVE form, always and without fail. This has nothing to do with the INTERESTED BYSTANDER usage – it's something entirely different.

B. The Principle of Substitution.
Languages, like automobiles, are made up of replaceable parts, but the part you substitute must fit the frame into which it is put. For example, in the frame Er kennt mich (He knows me), the Accusative form mich may be replaced only by other Accusative forms – that is, forms from the same horizontal line in the table of pronoun forms as mich, the line labeled ‘ACCUSATIVE forms’. Similarly, Dative forms must be replaced by other Dative forms, and Nominative forms by other Nominative forms.
Er kennt mich / uns / ihn / es / sie / sie / Sie / wen? (He knows me / us / him / it / her / them / you / whom?)
Ich gehe oft ins Kino mit ihr / ihm / ihnen. (I often go to the movies with her / him / them.)
Kennen Sie Herrn Becker? wir / sie? (Do you know Mr. Becker? we / they?)

C. Verb forms and functions – The Present
Forms.
In German, and in English, when you substitute one Nominative form for another, that is, change the SUBJECT in a sentence, you sometimes have to change the form of the verb as well. The subject and the verb have to fit together. Note the following English forms: I, you, we, they sing, do (no ending); he, it, she sings, does (ending -s).

All but a very few German verbs have the following forms:
ich komme, gebe (ending -e)
er, es, sie kommt, gibt (ending -t)
wir, sie ('they'), Sie kommen, geben (ending -en)

Note that German verbs have a special form with the pronoun ich. Otherwise the pronouns and verbs are grouped as they are in English. Notice that the vowel in the stem of geben appears as i: in the er-form: er gibt. This is something like the English says or does versus say or do, except that in German the vowel-change is shown even more clearly in the writing system. There are several verbs in German that have this kind of irregular er-form, but there is no simple way of determining which verbs they are. They are not very numerous however, and we’ll point them out as we encounter them.

Two German verbs you have encountered show a very slight modification in the er-form. They are arbeiten and kosten. After a -t- (or a -d-) a connecting vowel -e- occurs before the ending -t so that the ending is heard distinctly: er arbeitet; er kostet.

We have four verbs so far that exhibit the following pattern:
ich kann, darf, muss, will (no ending)
er kann, darf, muss, will
wir können, dürfen, müssen, wollen (ending -en)
There are three more verbs with the same pattern, making a total of seven in all. Notice that the English equivalents of the verbs listed above have no -s ending in the he form: he can, he may, he must, and he will (in the sense of he insists).

The following forms of haben ‘to have’, sein ‘to be’ and möchte(n) ‘would like to’ complete the inventory:
ich habe, bin, möchte
he hat, ist, möchte
wir haben, sind, möchten
The patterns of the first two of these verbs are unique and are found in no other German verbs. The forms möchte and möchten are special forms which we will deal with later.

Here is a table of verb forms (pattern A and B special forms):
ich komme, treffe, habe, bin, kann
he kommt, trifft, hat, ist
wir kommen, treffen, können, haben, sind, möchte, möchten
All verbs in German follow pattern A or pattern B except the nine indicated and one more that is still to come.

Functions.
English uses a verb form with the ending -ing very freely: he’s singing, we're waiting, it’s raining. German has no corresponding form and uses the simple form of the verb for such expressions: er gibt; gibt er? (he gives; is he giving? does he give?).

For commands, German uses the verb form with the ending -en followed by the pronoun Sie. The German form is like Biblical English: 'Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel…'. Please speak slowly. Show me your luggage please. Bitte sprechen Sie langsam. zeigen Sie mir bitte Ihr Gepäck.

Two verb forms can be used together in German or in English as a phrase. Although German doesn't have verb phrases like ‘is going’ or ‘does believe’, it has others:
Ich möchte gern Wasser haben.
Können Sie mich gut verstehen?
Darf ich Ihren Pass sehen?
Sie müssen zum Zoll gehen.
I'd like to have water. Can you understand me well? May I see your passport? You have to go to the customs office.
The second part of the German verb phrase comes at the end of the sentence and is called the infinitive. It is the form with the ending -en, but it never has a subject and is unaffected by any change of subject: Ich kann gehen. Wir können gehen. There is only one irregular infinitive in German: sein 'to be'; the infinitive of every other verb is the same as the wir-form.

III. List of verbs in units 1 and 2:
Pattern A: arbeite, besuche, bleibe, gehe, arbeitet, besucht, bleibt, geht, arbeiten, besuchen, bleiben, gehen, gehöre, glaube, heisse, kenne, gehört, glaubt, heisst, kennt, gehören, glauben, heissen, kennen, komme, (koste), kommt, kostet, kommen, kosten.
Pattern B: esse, gebe, sehe, isst, gibt, sieht, essen, geben, sehen, sage, verstehe, sagt, versteht, sagen, verstehen, spreche, treffe, spricht, trifft, sprechen, treffen, wohne, wohnt, wohnen, fahre, fährt, fahren, zeige, zeigt, zeigen, gefalle, gefällt, gefallen.

D. hin and her.
Wo wohnen Sie? Wo kommen Sie her? Wo gehen Sie hin? (Where do you live? Where do you come from? Where are you going to?)
Wo by itself means ‘where?’ in the sense of ‘in what place?’. To give it the meaning ‘where from?’ the little word her is added; to give it the meaning ‘where to?’ the little word hin is added. The position of hin and her is usually at the end of the sentence or question. They may occur alternately however at the beginning after wo. The writing system joins hin and her to the preceding question word or adverb: Woher? ‘Where from?’; Wohin? ‘Where to?’; dahin, dorthin ‘to there’. Wo fahren Sie heute hin? Where are you going today? Wohin fahren Sie heute? Wir fahren dorthin. (We are going there.)
